items.text: WTI crude surged 9.6% to $91.48/bbl and Brent rose 8.7% to $96.02/bbl as of Sept 1, driven by Middle East geopolitical tensions and supply concerns. This energy shock is feeding direct inflation expectations in consumer surveys and threatening refinancing costs for oil-dependent corporates and levered energy credits.

July payrolls printed -23K (vs consensus +20K), a shocking reversal that signals labor market deceleration despite stable unemployment at 4.1%. Initial claims inched to 206K. This erosion of demand-side labor momentum—combined with wage growth (AHE) cooling to 3.15%—pressures consumer balance sheets and weakens the foundation for debt service capacity across consumer-facing credit.

Headline CPI moderated to 3.3% YoY and core to 2.47% YoY in July, but PPI remained elevated at 4.66% and energy prices are re-accelerating. National average gasoline prices held above $4 a gallon across August, and consumers expect higher prices at the pump in the future. Sticky inflation in services and energy keeps real yields elevated, pressuring asset values and high-yield spreads.

Fed funds held at 3.75% as of Sept 3, and the 10Y TSY yield rose 12bp to 4.79% with the 2Y at 4.39%, tightening the curve to 43bp. ECB deposit rate stands at 2.25% effective June 17, with traders pricing in potential further hikes later in 2026. Rates are not cutting; duration and refinancing risk remain elevated globally.

HY OAS blew out 6bp to 266bp, IG OAS moved 2bp wider to 81bp, and CCC OAS jumped 27bp to 1053bp (per latest FRED data Sept 2). Credit is re-pricing higher geopolitical risk and tightening labor dynamics; high-yield and distressed credits face renewed pressure on both spreads and recovery assumptions.

GDPNow nowcast surged to 4.7% (from 1.54% prior), but Q2 actual GDP printed 1.5% (down from 2.1% prior). The gap signals front-loaded consumer pull-forward and tariff-related anomalies; Q3 momentum is likely to moderate sharply as energy shock, labor weakness, and sentiment collapse filter through real demand.

Michigan consumer sentiment was revised to 51.7 in August from July's 55.2, down about 6% and roughly 11% below year-ago levels, reflecting persistent inflation concerns. Housing starts fell to 1,239K from 1,415K prior, and existing home sales declined to 4.06M from 4.13M. Consumer distress is mounting; housing roll-overs and weakening affordability threaten mortgage-backed credit and consumer leverage across retail credits.

themeCards.title: Middle East Energy Shock
themeCards.statusLine: WTI and Brent crude up 9.6% and 8.7% respectively; geopolitical tension crimping supply and hiking headline inflation expectations. Consumer sentiment has plunged (UMich 51.7 vs 55.2 prior) as households front-run fuel cost expectations amid Middle East conflict.
themeCards.relevance: Special situations credit investors face repricing of commodity-linked issuers, energy credits (both producers and refiners), and airlines/transportation. CCC spreads already at +1053bp signal market stress; selective distress likely among levered energy names and supply-chain-exposed credits.

themeCards.title: Labor Market Sudden Deterioration
themeCards.statusLine: July nonfarm payrolls crashed -23K vs consensus +20K; unemployment holding at 4.1% masks sharp deceleration in hiring. Average hourly earnings growth slowed to 3.15% from 3.41%.
themeCards.relevance: This is a material credit negative. Weakening labor demand erodes consumer purchasing power and debt-service capacity precisely when debt levels are elevated and refinancing risk is acute. Watch for uptick in defaults among consumer cyclicals, retail credits, and lower-rated consumer finance originators.

themeCards.title: Consumer Sentiment Collapse
themeCards.statusLine: UMich sentiment fell to 51.0 preliminary (revised 51.7 final) in August, down 7.6% MoM from 55.2, lowest since energy shock in late 2024, driven by inflation fears and weaker economic outlook.
themeCards.relevance: Consumer credit stress is broadening: only 8% of consumers expect income to outpace inflation. Auto loans, credit card portfolios, and subprime credit are vulnerable. Rising delinquencies and loss severity on consumer ABS and RMBS will pressure valuations.

themeCards.title: Curve Steepening & Refinancing Wall
themeCards.statusLine: 2-10 curve at 43bp (up from 39bp prior); 10Y yield at 4.79% and 2Y at 4.39%. Refinancing calendar remains heavy through 2026–27 for both corporates and CLOs, with rates locked in at higher levels.
themeCards.relevance: Corporate high-yield and leveraged credit refinancing becomes materially more expensive; default risk rises for names with near-term maturity walls or covenant tightness. Watch for CLO asset turnover and wall mechanics under stress; floating-rate exposure becomes a key risk/return driver.

themeCards.title: China Manufacturing Contraction
themeCards.statusLine: Official manufacturing PMI at 49.8 in August (up from 49.2 in July) signals continued contraction despite sequential improvement; Caixin PMI at 51.5 shows export momentum but confidence at lowest since January due to domestic demand weakness.
themeCards.relevance: Two-speed China (exports expanding, domestic contracting) pressures commodity valuations and emerging-market corporate credits reliant on Chinese demand. Supply-chain dislocations and margin compression for China-exposed multinationals increase default risk in vulnerable credit names.

themeCards.title: Manufacturing PMI Divergence (US)
themeCards.statusLine: ISM Manufacturing PMI fell to 54.6 in August (below 55.2 consensus), marking the eighth consecutive month of expansion but with new orders collapsing sharply to 53.7 from 56.7. ISM Services PMI expanded to 55.4 in August, up 1.3 points from July, marking 26 consecutive months of expansion.
themeCards.relevance: Manufacturing demand is rolling over while services remain resilient—a classic late-cycle, consumption-driven profile. Credit investors must distinguish between goods-exposed credits (facing inventory destocking, margin compression) and services-dependent credits (still supported by labor income and consumer spending, but now at risk as sentiment has collapsed).

ecb.delta: up from 2.0% in April, holding steady in July, market pricing one more 25bp hike by year-end

chinaPMI.delta: up 0.6 points from 49.2 in July but still in contraction; private (Caixin) PMI at 51.5 signals export resilience offsetting domestic weakness

ismServices.delta: beat August expectations, up 1.3 points from 54.1 in July; 26th consecutive month of expansion

retailSales.delta: better than expected; YoY retail ex-autos at 5.75% as of July

existingHome.delta: down from 4.13M in June; 6.9% below year-ago; housing market softening evident

consensus.PCE: Pending next release (last reading: 3.7% headline, 3.34% core in July)
consensus.PPI: Pending next release (last reading: 4.66% in July)
consensus.Retail Sales: Pending August release; July was +0.9% m/m, YoY at +5.0%
consensus.ISM Mfg: August printed 54.6 (consensus 55.2); next release early October
consensus.ISM Services: August printed 55.4 (no consensus forecasted); next release early October
consensus.GDP: Q2 actual 1.5% (vs consensus ~1.8%); GDPNow nowcast 4.7% for Q3 (pending revision)

regime.label: Late-cycle stagflationary impulse
regime.detail: Energy shock resurfacing inflation, labor softening, consumer sentiment collapsing, credit spreads widening, growth momentum at risk of sharp deceleration in Q3–Q4.
